findings.title: Typing in the Log-activity title field crashes the whole app to a blank page (setState updater reads event.currentTarget after dispatch)
findings.location: app/ITrackApp.tsx:4521-4523 (setActivityDraft((current) => ({...current, title: event.currentTarget.value}))); same pattern at 4549-4551, 4592-4593, 4630-4632, 4749-4751
findings.evidence: Production build (dist Aug 12, served by workerd on :8788): opened Log activity, typed 'Advanced cardiac life support renewal course 2026' at 60 ms/keystroke into 'Course, conference, or activity'. Result in 2/2 runs (CPU 1x and 4x): console 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading value) at ITrackApp-cj8gPdG6.js:4:69125' + 'The above error occurred in a React component', dialog gone, document.body.innerText empty; screenshot typing-prodbuild-cpu1-60ms.png is a blank page. Same error reproduced on the dev server (localhost:3000, ITrackApp.tsx transformed line 3066 = `title: event.currentTarget.value` inside the updater) and in the 30 ms-delay interaction runs. React nulls currentTarget after the listener returns; when a keystroke arrives while a render is pending the updater runs later during render and dereferences null. Found while measuring long tasks during the Log-activity interaction; it is a correctness bug, not a perf cost, but it breaks the core flow.
findings.impact: Any user who types at a normal pace into the activity title (and likely the credits/units/provider fields that use the same pattern) loses the sheet and the whole screen; they must reload and the in-memory form is gone. This blocks the primary logging flow on a public self-serve product.
findings.recommendation: Read the value synchronously and close over it: `const value = event.currentTarget.value; setActivityDraft((current) => ({ ...current, title: value }))`, and apply the same change at the other four sites (4549, 4592, 4630, 4749). Add a Playwright test that types 50 characters at 0-60 ms delay into each draft field and asserts no pageerror and the dialog stays open. Worth wrapping the sheet in an error boundary so a future field bug degrades to a toast instead of a blank page.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced on the dev server (localhost:3000) and on the production build of HEAD 3f477e6 served under wrangler on :8789; Railway's latest SUCCESS deployment (b8b32146, 2026-08-12 12:24 UTC) is that same commit, so this is live. It is WORSE than described: the crash is deterministic on the SECOND keystroke at any typing speed (tested 30/60/120/300/400/500 ms per key) - keystroke 1 renders, keystroke 2 throws 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading value)' at ITrackApp-cj8gPdG6.js:4:69125 and the prod page goes fully blank (document.body.innerText length 0; typing-prodbuild-title-crash.png). Reproduced in title, totalUnits and provider; allocatedUnits accepted '12.5' without crashing in my run; completionDate (same pattern) not exercised. Cited lines verified (4523, 4551, 4593, 4632, 4751). No error boundary exists under app/. Playwright fill() emits a single input event and never triggers it, which is why existing tests pass. Mechanism: React nulls event.currentTarget after the listener returns; the first update is computed eagerly inside the handler, the second is deferred to render, where the updater dereferences null. Fix as recommended (capture value synchronously).

findings.title: Service-worker offline fallback is broken: precached /offline.html is a 307 redirect, so offline navigation ends in net::ERR_FAILED
findings.location: public/sw.js:6-12 (PRECACHE '/offline.html') and :244-261 (navigate handler returns cache.match('/offline.html')); Workers static-asset html_handling turns /offline.html into 307 -> /offline
findings.evidence: GET /offline.html on the production build returns 'HTTP/1.1 307 Temporary Redirect, Location: /offline' (GET /offline is 200). cache.addAll follows the redirect and stores a redirected response; Chrome refuses to answer a navigation with a redirected cached response. Playwright with the SW active and controlling (controller=true, cache license-lantern-static-v3 populated with /offline.html), context.setOffline(true), page.goto('/history') -> 'net::ERR_FAILED' (prodbuild-desktop-light.json 'offline' block, prodbuild-desktop-light-offline-nav.png). The crafted offline.html (4.3 KB) is never shown.
findings.impact: The one thing the offline-first SW promises (a branded 'you are offline, reconnect' page) fails and users on flaky mobile networks get the browser's error page; the precache also still spends bytes on it. If web push stays, the SW stays, so this remains user-visible.
findings.recommendation: Precache and match the canonical URL '/offline' (or fetch '/offline.html' with redirect:'follow' and store `new Response(await res.arrayBuffer(), { headers: res.headers })` so the stored response is not marked redirected). Add a Playwright offline test. If the redesign drops the SW entirely (no push), delete sw.js and the registration effect instead.
findings.verifier_note: Mechanism confirmed on the prod build: GET /offline.html -> 307 Location: /offline; the SW cache entry for /offline.html has redirected:true (response url /offline); with the SW controlling and context offline, goto('/history') and goto('/offline') both end in net::ERR_FAILED (pv-offline.cjs, offline-nav-prodbuild.png). Downgraded because the only loss is the branded 'you are offline' page versus Chrome's own offline page - the app has no offline functionality to lose, and precache still succeeds. Trivial fix (precache '/offline' or re-wrap the response); moot if the SW is dropped with push.

findings.title: Single 496 KB client bundle + 97 KB stylesheet gate hydration on mobile; ~70% of JS and ~73% of CSS is unused on the first screen
findings.location: dist/client/assets/ITrackApp-cj8gPdG6.js (230 KB / 58.5 KB gz), framework-BOexRV2D.js (185 KB / 58 KB gz), index-w_ofqVGk.js (79 KB / 24 KB gz), index-C0H0qL7m.css (97 KB / 19 KB gz, render-blocking); app/page.tsx:1 and app/credentials/page.tsx:1 import the whole app/ITrackApp.tsx (10,953 lines, one 'use client' component); app/globals.css (6,618 lines)
findings.evidence: Cold load = 9 requests, 224 KB wire / 675 KB decoded; JS is 142 KB gz of it. Chrome coverage on the home screen: ITrackApp 29% used, framework 35%, vinext index 23%, CSS 27% (prodbuild-cov-desktop-light.summary.txt). Trace on 4x CPU + Fast 3G (1.6 Mbps/150 ms): CSS 166->711 ms, ITrackApp chunk 167->1,232 ms, FCP (skeleton) 773-780 ms, hydrated 1,291-1,293 ms, data painted 1,512-1,518 ms, LCP 1,565-1,582 ms; main thread busy only 590-648 ms, no task >= 50 ms (prodbuild-mobile-cpu4-fast3g-trace-*.summary.txt). Desktop unthrottled: FCP 46 ms, hydrated 47 ms, data 65 ms, LCP 97 ms. Warm navigation: all 6 assets served from cache/SW, only /api/workspace (3.3 KB) fetched, data painted at 39 ms.
findings.impact: On a mid-range phone on a poor connection the user stares at a skeleton for ~1.3 s and sees real data at ~1.5 s; roughly 0.5 s of that is waiting for JS that the first screen does not execute. Runtime cost is fine (no long tasks), so this is purely a byte/priority problem and it will grow with every added screen unless the redesign splits by screen.
findings.recommendation: Make the planned screen decomposition a code-splitting exercise: route-level lazy chunks for Credentials/History/Profile/credential detail, and lazy sheets for Log activity, the template chooser and reminders; budget <= 60 KB gz JS and <= 8 KB gz CSS for the Home first paint. Inline the skeleton's critical CSS in the shell and ship per-screen CSS (or purge unused Tailwind/utility rules) so FCP no longer waits for the full stylesheet competing with 5 modulepreloads. Keep the vinext modulepreload for the Home chunk only.
findings.verifier_note: All numbers reproduced: cold load 9 requests, 224.1 KB wire / 674.5 KB decoded; byte-accurate coverage on Home = ITrackApp 29%, framework 34%, vinext index 23%, CSS 27% (coverage-desktop-home.txt); 4x CPU + 1.6 Mbps/150 ms: FCP 752-784 ms, data paint 1510-1526 ms, LCP 1536-1560 ms across 4 runs; desktop FCP 64 / data 85 / LCP 116 ms. Downgraded: LCP 1.55 s under the Lighthouse mobile profile is 'good' (<2.5 s), so it does not materially hurt users today; it is a budget to carry into the redesign. Two corrections: prod passes Brotli through (content-encoding: br verified on itrackceu.com/api/widget-summary) and Chrome only negotiates br over HTTPS, so real-world critical bytes are ~15% below the gzip figures quoted (my br11 estimate 138.6 KB vs 162.6 KB gz9 for all shell assets); and warm navigations already serve every asset from cache (0 wire).

findings.title: Workspace data is fetched only after hydration (client-side waterfall): HTML -> JS -> hydrate -> /api/workspace -> paint
findings.location: app/ITrackApp.tsx:2100-2105 (useEffect -> setTimeout(loadWorkspace, 0)) and :1934 (fetch('/api/workspace', cache:'no-store')); app/page.tsx (force-dynamic, renders <ITrackApp/> with no data); LoadingDashboard at app/ITrackApp.tsx:10853-10878 is what the server renders
findings.evidence: SSR HTML (13.4 KB) contains only the sidebar and the 'Loading your renewal workspace' skeleton (224 visible characters). Trace on 4x CPU + Fast 3G: hydrated at 1,291 ms, /api/workspace request 1,297->1,474 ms, workspace painted 1,512 ms, i.e. ~220 ms (one RTT + server) spent after the JS was already there; desktop: hydrated 47 ms -> data 65 ms. The API itself is cheap: 9-11 ms warm, 99 ms on the very first request after a worker start (schema + catalog-fingerprint check), 12-14 KB raw / 3.1-3.3 KB gz for the seeded demo. The task mentioned a known deferred 'SSR/first-paint waterfall (architectural)' item; I could not find that wording in docs/ or git history (only 'Phase 2 (explicitly deferred)' for Stripe/ads in docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-11-itrack-public-signup.md:2196), but the waterfall is real and measured.
findings.impact: Every cold load and every full reload pays an extra network round trip before real content, and LCP (the first credential heading) is pinned behind it; on mobile that is ~0.2-0.4 s of skeleton after the JS has already arrived.
findings.recommendation: When Home is rebuilt as its own screen, fetch the workspace on the server (the route already has the identity headers; call getWorkspace in the server component and pass it as props / stream it) so the first HTML contains data and the client only hydrates. Cheapest interim: emit `<link rel="preload" as="fetch" href="/api/workspace" crossorigin>` from the layout and keep the client fetch, which starts the request in parallel with the JS download.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced: SSR HTML is 13,406 B containing only the 'Loading your renewal workspace' skeleton plus 5 modulepreloads; on the throttled mobile profile the JS chunks finish at ~1,250 ms, /api/workspace runs 1,293-1,300 -> 1,474 ms and data paints at 1,510-1,526 ms (~230 ms of skeleton after the JS is present); desktop 56 -> 71 ms. useEffect -> setTimeout(loadWorkspace, 0) and fetch('/api/workspace', cache:'no-store') verified at ITrackApp.tsx ~1934/2100. Server-fetch or preload as recommended when Home is rebuilt.

findings.title: 57 KB PNG favicon on the critical path, ~397 KB of icon precache on first visit, and all public/ images served with max-age=0
findings.location: app/layout.tsx:31-42 (icons: icon-192.png and icon-512.png used as favicon), public/icon-192.png (192px, 58,066 B), public/icon-512.png (512px, 284,474 B), public/apple-touch-icon.png (51,438 B), public/og.png (2400x1260, 262,183 B); public/_headers (rules only for /sw.js and /assets/*); public/sw.js:6-12 PRECACHE; app/ITrackApp.tsx:2121-2134 registers the SW during hydration effects
findings.evidence: Every cold app load requests /icon-192.png (56.9 KB wire, no compression possible) as the tab icon; on the 4x/Fast-3G trace it downloads 753->1,403 ms, overlapping the framework/ITrackApp chunks (which finish at 1,219-1,239 ms). The SW install then precaches offline.html + manifest + icon-192 (57 KB) + icon-512 (284 KB) + apple-touch-icon (51 KB) = ~397 KB in the background during onboarding (verified cache entries). All four PNGs are 8-bit, no alpha, and served 'Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate' (measured on the identical build), so non-SW browsers revalidate them through the proxy each visit (~150-250 ms RTT from NYC). No SVG/ICO favicon exists.
findings.impact: On a 1.6 Mbps link the favicon alone steals ~275 ms of bandwidth while hydration is waiting for JS, and the precache steals ~2 s more during the user's first minutes; a 512px icon is only needed by the OS at install time.
findings.recommendation: Add a ~1 KB SVG (or 32/48px ICO) favicon and reference it first in metadata.icons; run the PNGs through oxipng/pngquant (typically 60-80% smaller) and, if the redesign changes the brand mark, regenerate them at that time; add `/icon-*.png`, `/apple-touch-icon.png`, `/og.png`: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400` and `/ocr/*: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` (versioned by the tesseract release) to public/_headers; trim PRECACHE to the offline page and icon-192 only; register the SW after the workspace has painted (requestIdleCallback / after firstWorkspacePaint) instead of in the first effect.
findings.verifier_note: Bytes verified: /icon-192.png (58,066 B) is requested on every cold load as the tab icon (765 -> 1,422 ms on the throttled trace), all four PNGs are 8-bit RGB served 'public, max-age=0, must-revalidate', the SW precaches offline.html + manifest + 3 icons (~399 KB), and the SW registers in a mount effect right after hydration. The critical-path claim is overstated: a clean A/B on the same 4x CPU / Fast-3G profile (route-abort the icon) moved data paint from 1510/1511 to 1414/1416 ms and LCP from 1544/1536 to 1452/1440 ms, i.e. ~95-100 ms, not ~275 ms. The precache's bandwidth competition could not be demonstrated (SW-initiated fetches bypass DevTools throttling; first-visit data paint 1524/1551 vs 1510 baseline). PIL palette recompression shows real headroom (icon-192 58->33 KB, icon-512 284->156 KB, og 262->119 KB) but not the 60-80% claimed without a proper optimizer. Worth doing, but ~0.1 s on slow mobile is polish.

findings.title: /api/catalog ships 702 KB (95 KB gz) to open the template chooser; the list needs ~48 KB and the ETag is recomputed by hashing 700 KB on every request
findings.location: app/api/catalog/route.ts:8-12, 38-47 (JSON.stringify(getRuleCatalog) + SHA-256 per request, incl. 304s); app/api/workspace/route.ts:4141 getRuleCatalog -> loadRuleCatalog; app/ITrackApp.tsx:1978-2008 loadCatalog (fetched when the chooser opens)
findings.evidence: Measured body 701,630 B raw / 95,413 B gzip; 170 templates, 827 categories; by field: categories 430,512 B, sourceTitle 199,682 B, sourceUrl 14 KB, credentialName 11 KB. A slim list (id, credentialName, profession, jurisdiction, issuer, totalUnits, unitLabel, cycleMonths) serialises to 47,951 B raw. Server time 12-15 ms for 200 and 10 ms for a 304 (it still builds and hashes the full body). Client: desktop click->response 32 ms, JS heap 4.0 -> 10.4 MB after parse, no long tasks; 4x CPU + Fast 3G: click->response 214 ms plus ~0.5 s of download for 95 KB, search keystrokes max 24 ms. Cache-Control private, max-age=900 so it is re-downloaded after 15 min.
findings.impact: The chooser is onboarding step 1 for every new user; on mobile it adds roughly half a second of spinner and 6 MB of heap for data (source titles, all category rules) that only matters after a template is picked.
findings.recommendation: Split into a slim list endpoint (~8 KB gz) plus per-template detail fetched on selection (or embed detail in createCredential's response); compute the ETag once from the existing managedCatalogFingerprint() instead of hashing the body per request; raise max-age (the catalog changes only on deploy) and make the client reuse the cached list across sessions. Fold this into the chooser screen rebuild.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced exactly on the prod build: 701,630 B raw / 95,413 B gz, 170 templates, categories 413 KB + sourceTitle 200 KB, slim list 47,472 B; 304 costs 9.3-9.8 ms vs 10.4-10.7 ms for a 200 because the ETag is hashed before the If-None-Match check (route.ts:40-42). One correction: the client fetch (ITrackApp.tsx:1984) uses the default cache mode, so the browser serves it from HTTP cache for 15 min and then revalidates with the ETag (304), it is not 're-downloaded after 15 min', and 'reuse across sessions' already happens via the HTTP cache. Real cost is 95 KB gz once per device per deploy (~0.5 s spinner on slow mobile) - keep as a chooser-rebuild item.

findings.title: First certificate scan silently downloads 4.45 MB (tesseract core + English model); no prefetch, no size disclosure, no immutable caching outside the SW
findings.location: app/lib/certificateOcr.ts:285-296 (dynamic import('tesseract.js'), workerPath /ocr/worker.min.js, corePath /ocr/core, langPath /ocr/lang); public/ocr/* (3 core variants x ~3.9 MB + eng.traineddata.gz 2.95 MB = 14.7 MB of the 16 MB client build); public/sw.js:13-20 runtime-caches them
findings.evidence: tesseract.js is correctly lazy: only assets/src-DEYky76Y.js (7.3 KB gz) loads when a file is chosen. The first scan then fetches worker.min.js 33.9 KB gz + tesseract-core-relaxedsimd-lstm.wasm.js 1,457,906 B gz + eng.traineddata.gz 2,952,873 B (already gzip, not re-compressed) = ~4.45 MB wire; all served 'max-age=0, must-revalidate' and cached only by the service worker (verified: second scan 0 bytes on the wire, cache entries present). Desktop unthrottled: file chosen -> 'Found 2 details' in 514 ms first time, 507 ms second time (ocr.json, ocr-attempt-1.png). At 1.6 Mbps the same download is ~22-25 s before recognition can start.
findings.impact: A stranger on mobile data who taps 'Take photo' waits tens of seconds on the first scan with only a progress label, and pays it again if their browser has no SW (Safari private mode) because the files revalidate; the on-device privacy story is right, but the cost is invisible until it bites.
findings.recommendation: Keep it lazy but (a) prefetch the OCR bundle with `<link rel=prefetch>`/cache.addAll when the Log-activity sheet opens on non-metered connections (navigator.connection.saveData === false, effectiveType === '4g'), (b) state '~4.5 MB one-time download' next to Take photo, (c) mark /ocr/* immutable in public/_headers (see perf-05) so HTTP cache covers non-SW browsers, and (d) drop the two unused core variants from the deploy or serve only the one tesseract selects (relaxedsimd in Chrome) to shrink the image.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced the scan on the prod build: only src-DEYky76Y.js (7 KB gz) loads when a file is chosen; the first scan populates the SW cache with /ocr/worker.min.js, tesseract-core-relaxedsimd-lstm.wasm.js (relaxedsimd confirmed as the chosen core) and eng.traineddata.gz; curl wire sizes 33,865 + 1,457,906 + 2,952,873 = 4,444,644 B gz (4.33 MB with br); all 'max-age=0, must-revalidate'; scan 516/512 ms on desktop, second scan 0 bytes from the SW. public/ocr is 14 MB of the build with three core variants; navigator.connection/saveData never consulted (grep). Recommendation stands.

findings.title: Build ships 181 KB of dead Manrope/Newsreader woff2 files, and the redesign's new display face needs a font-loading budget (today nothing loads)
findings.location: dist/client/assets/_vinext_fonts/manrope-76eca2803f7f/*.woff2 (6 files, 75 KB) and newsreader-94c054835b7e/*.woff2 (3 files, 106 KB), copied from the gitignored .vinext/fonts cache (its style.css still points at the old credential-lantern path); app/layout.tsx:99-103 and docs/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md 'Typography' document the system-stack decision (commit 47caef3)
findings.evidence: grep of every JS/CSS file in dist/client and dist/server for 'manrope|newsreader|_vinext_fonts' returns nothing; document.fonts in every Playwright run is empty ('none (system stack)'); the files are emitted purely because the .vinext/fonts cache survived the font removal. No user downloads them, so cost today is deploy-size and audit noise only.
findings.impact: Zero runtime impact now. The real exposure is forward-looking: the warm editorial redesign adds a display face, and with the current 142 KB gz JS on the critical path an unsubsetted 2-3-weight serif (80-150 KB) would push mobile FCP well past 1 s and reintroduce the render-blocking font round trip the current design explicitly removed.
findings.recommendation: Delete .vinext/fonts before the next build (cache dir, gitignored) and add it to the Docker build's clean step. For the redesign: self-host one or two woff2 subsets (latin only, variable or 2 weights, ~25-40 KB total), `font-display: swap` with a metric-matched fallback (size-adjust/ascent-override) so there is no layout shift, preload only the face used above the fold, and keep body text on the system stack or a single subset.
findings.verifier_note: Verified: 9 woff2 files = 181,136 B under dist/client/assets/_vinext_fonts; grep for manrope|newsreader|_vinext_fonts across dist/client and dist/server (js/css/html) returns nothing; .vinext/fonts cache is present with a style.css still declaring Manrope; layout.tsx has no font className. Hygiene-only: nothing requests these files, so cost is image size and audit noise; the font-budget guidance for the redesign is advice, not a defect.

findings.title: Gateway/landing delivery hygiene: public pages uncompressed and no-store, anonymous 401 for favicon/robots/og/manifest, duplicate Railway hostname, www does not resolve
findings.location: deploy/railway/gateway.mjs:45-54 (servePage: no content-encoding, cache-control no-store, no ETag), :185-215 (any non-HTML anonymous GET, e.g. /favicon.ico, /robots.txt, /og.png, /manifest.webmanifest, gets 401 Basic); deploy/railway/pages/landing.html:4-7 (no <link rel=icon>, no og:image); DNS for www.itrackceu.com
findings.evidence: curl with a Safari UA + Accept-Encoding gzip,br: landing 200, 7,723 B, no content-encoding, cache-control no-store, no ETag, TTFB 157/219/255 ms, healthz 175/257/175 ms (so proxy overhead is negligible). Playwright landing: 2 requests, FCP=LCP 456 ms desktop / 368 ms mobile-throttled, CLS 0, DOM 66 nodes; the second request is /favicon.ico -> 401 (console error). /robots.txt, /sitemap.xml, /og.png, /manifest.webmanifest, /icon-512.png, /sw.js -> 401 for anonymous clients. https://itrack-production-da8b.up.railway.app/ serves the identical landing with no canonical/redirect. www.itrackceu.com: 'Could not resolve host'. Worker-proxied responses do keep gzip (/api/widget-summary 401 body has content-encoding: gzip), so compression is only missing for the five gateway pages (26.8 KB total).
findings.impact: Performance impact is small (the landing is lean; gzip would save ~5 KB and a validator would let back/forward reuse it), but the 401s mean crawlers and link unfurlers cannot fetch robots/og/favicon, the tab shows no icon, and anyone typing www. gets a hard failure, which mostly hurts SEO/trust (other dimensions) rather than speed.
findings.recommendation: In gateway.mjs add a small public allowlist proxied without auth (/favicon.ico, /favicon.svg, /icon-*.png, /apple-touch-icon.png, /og.png, /manifest.webmanifest, /robots.txt, /sitemap.xml, /.well-known/*), gzip the cached page buffers once at startup and serve with an ETag and `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300` (the pages are static), 301 the railway.app host to itrackceu.com, add a www CNAME + redirect, and give landing.html a `<link rel=icon>` and og:image tags.
findings.verifier_note: All sub-claims verified against prod with a Safari UA: landing 200, 7,723 B, no content-encoding despite 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, br', cache-control: no-store, no ETag, TTFB 106-186 ms vs /healthz 109-173 ms (proxy overhead negligible); anonymous /favicon.ico, /robots.txt, /sitemap.xml, /og.png, /manifest.webmanifest, /icon-192.png, /sw.js, /offline.html all 401 (23 B); /history -> 303 /login; itrack-production-da8b.up.railway.app serves the identical landing with no redirect; www.itrackceu.com has no DNS record; landing.html contains zero rel= links (no icon, no og:image); gateway.mjs lines 45-54 and 185-215 match. Worker responses do keep br/gzip through the proxy. Perf impact is small; the crawler/unfurl/trust consequences belong to SEO/landing dimensions.

findings.title: Service worker serves icons, manifest, og image and the 4.4 MB OCR bundle cache-first forever under a constant cache name, so a redeploy with a new brand mark or a tesseract upgrade never reaches installed users
findings.location: public/sw.js:5 (CACHE_NAME 'license-lantern-static-v3'), :13-21 (CACHEABLE_STATIC_PATHS), :35-42 (precache only at install), :264-276 (cache-first, no expiry or revalidation)
findings.evidence: Experiment on the production build (pv-stale.cjs): with the SW installed and controlling, fetch('/icon-192.png') returned 58,066 B ETag 92c8da66...; I then replaced icon-192.png in the served copy (direct server response became 51,438 B, ETag d26b09bb...), reloaded the page, and the page still received the old 58,066 B / old-ETag icon from the SW cache. The precache re-runs only when sw.js bytes change (updateViaCache none + byte comparison), and the runtime handler returns cache.match() before ever consulting the network; the same path covers /manifest.webmanifest, /og.png, /ocr/worker.min.js, the core wasm and eng.traineddata.gz.
findings.impact: The redesign will change the icons/manifest, and any tesseract.js upgrade changes worker.min.js/core; existing installs will keep the stale icons and, for OCR, can end up pairing a new src chunk with the old worker/core until someone edits sw.js. Nothing on the server can expire these entries.
findings.recommendation: Derive CACHE_NAME from a build hash injected at build time (or bump it on every asset change as a release step), switch manifest/icons to stale-while-revalidate, and serve the OCR bundle from versioned paths (/ocr/<tesseract-version>/...) with immutable headers so both the SW and HTTP caches key on content.

findings.title: History renders every activity in one pass with no pagination or windowing, and the full activity history rides in every /api/workspace response that each mutation refetches
findings.location: app/ITrackApp.tsx history view (rows rendered from workspace.activities; 10 loadWorkspace() call sites refetch the whole payload) and app/api/workspace/route.ts:5210 (getWorkspace returns all activities)
findings.evidence: Seeded 300 activities on one credential for identity perf-verify@example.com on the production build: /api/workspace grew from 11,871 B to 288,349 B raw (21,208 B gz, 29-35 ms server; ~920 B per activity). At 4x CPU on a 390x844 viewport: History tab rendered all 300 rows -> 7,668 DOM nodes with one 164 ms long task; opening the Log-activity sheet over it took 337 ms with a 123 ms long task; the first keystroke's input event lasted 48-56 ms (37-46 ms processing) because each keystroke re-renders the whole 11k-line component including the list. JSON.parse of the payload was only 0.8 ms, so the cost is DOM/render, not parsing (scale-history-mobile.png).
findings.impact: New users start empty so nothing is slow today, but cost is linear in history length and every keystroke and mutation pays it; a multi-year user with ~1,000 activities would be around 1 MB raw per refetch and ~25k DOM nodes on History, with visible hitches on mid-range phones.
findings.recommendation: When History becomes its own screen, window or paginate the list ('show more' or virtualization), move activity history behind its own cursor-paginated endpoint instead of the workspace blob, and have mutations return the changed rows so the client patches state rather than refetching everything.

findings.title: Widget feed leaks the oldest account's data to any holder of one shared static token (live in prod)
findings.location: deploy/railway/gateway.mjs:9,146-149 (WIDGET_FEED_PATH auth bypass) + app/api/widget-summary/route.ts:59-61 (SELECT id FROM users ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 1) + app/lib/widgetSummary.ts:13-23,175-190
findings.evidence: The gateway routes /api/widget-summary to the worker with identity=null and keepAuthorization=true, skipping all Basic/session auth. The worker authorizes with a single shared ITRACK_WIDGET_TOKEN (constant-time compare) then, with no per-user identity in the request, picks the FIRST user row (ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 1) and returns that user's per-credential name, dueDate, daysToRenewal, creditsDone/Required and readinessPercent. The route comment still asserts 'iTrack is a single-user install', which is false now that strangers self-serve sign up. Prod check: GET https://itrackceu.com/api/widget-summary with no Authorization returns HTTP 401 (not 503), so ITRACK_WIDGET_TOKEN IS configured in production (see prod_headers.txt) — the feed is live. The token's purpose was to ship inside the iOS WidgetKit extension, i.e. it lives in distributed client binaries and is extractable.
findings.impact: Anyone who obtains the one shared widget token (extractable from shipped iOS builds) can read the first-registered user's professional credential names, renewal deadlines, and progress — always the same fixed victim, never the caller's own data — a cross-tenant personal-data exposure on a now-public multi-user SaaS.
findings.recommendation: Because the iOS shell is being retired, remove the endpoint (app/api/widget-summary), the gateway WIDGET_FEED_PATH exemption, and unset ITRACK_WIDGET_TOKEN in Railway. If a widget is ever revived, it must resolve the workspace from the authenticated caller's identity, never 'first user', and use per-install tokens bound to a user.
findings.verifier_note: Verified all three legs. gateway.mjs:146-149 routes /api/widget-summary with identity=null + keepAuthorization=true (auth bypass); route.ts:59-61 selects `SELECT id FROM users ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 1` with NO per-caller identity and returns that one user's credential names/dueDates/progress. Prod returns HTTP 401 (not 503) to a wrong/absent bearer, and Railway env confirms ITRACK_WIDGET_TOKEN IS set (value present in service vars) -> feed is live. Railway HTTP logs show /api/widget-summary is actively polled in prod (steady 401s every ~70s), so this is an exercised endpoint. I deliberately did NOT replay the real token to exfiltrate a live user's PII. Nuances that do not change P1: blast radius is one FIXED user (the earliest-created row, currently most likely the owner) not the caller; the token is 256-bit and shipped only in a private TestFlight build, so it is extractable-by-testers rather than public. It remains a live cross-tenant PII exposure behind a client-extractable shared secret, and the fix is trivial given iOS retirement.

findings.title: No security headers on prod landing or app (no HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy)
findings.location: deploy/railway/gateway.mjs:45-54 (servePage) and :95-124 (proxy passes worker headers through unchanged); next.config.ts (no headers()); no middleware.ts in repo
findings.evidence: servePage sets only content-type + cache-control; proxy forwards workerResponse.headers verbatim and adds none. A repo-wide grep for Strict-Transport-Security/Content-Security-Policy/X-Frame-Options/Referrer-Policy/Permissions-Policy finds them ONLY on the packet and evidence-download responses, never on the app shell or the public pages. Confirmed on prod (prod_headers.txt): GET / (Safari UA) and /credentials return none of these headers; the session cookie is Secure+HttpOnly but there is no HSTS.
findings.impact: The authenticated app can be framed (clickjacking) with no X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors; a first-visit MITM can attempt SSL-strip with no HSTS; there is no CSP to contain any XSS; and no Referrer-Policy/Permissions-Policy. This is the public conversion + data surface of a SaaS handling personal license data.
findings.recommendation: Add a hardening header set both in the gateway (servePage for landing/login/signup/reset/verify, and injected onto proxied responses) or via next.config headers(): Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload, X-Frame-Options: DENY (or CSP frame-ancestors 'none'), Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, Permissions-Policy minimal, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and a Content-Security-Policy for the app shell.
findings.verifier_note: Verified on prod (prod_headers_verify.txt): GET / (Safari UA), /login, /signup, /reset, /verify, and /credentials (303) return only content-type + cache-control; none of HSTS/CSP/X-Frame-Options/Referrer-Policy/Permissions-Policy/X-Content-Type-Options are present. Code confirms: servePage sets only 2 headers, proxy() pipes worker headers verbatim, next.config.ts has no headers(), no middleware.ts exists; the only security headers in the repo are on evidence-download/export/packet responses. TLS is 1.3 and http->https 301s, but hstspreload.org reports itrackceu.com status 'unknown' (not preloaded) and no HSTS header is served, so first-visit SSL-strip and clickjacking of the authenticated app are both open. One correction: redesign_relation should be fix_regardless, not carry_into_redesign — response headers are orthogonal to the visual redesign and should be added now.

findings.title: Verify-by-GET both consumes the single-use token and mints a session (mail-scanner hostile, GET side effect)
findings.location: deploy/railway/gateway.mjs:163-173 (GET /verify -> store.verifyEmail(token) + authRoutes.issueSessionCookie + 303 /)
findings.evidence: A GET to /verify?token=... calls verifyEmail (which marks the token used_at and cannot be replayed, see auth.mjs:105-116,145-153) and, on success, immediately issues a signed session cookie and redirects to /. Corporate mail security (Microsoft SafeLinks, Proofpoint, antivirus link scanners) routinely prefetch links in inbound email.
findings.impact: A scanner/prefetcher silently burns the verification token before the human clicks, so the real user lands on verify.html's 'invalid or already used' error and must use resend. Separately, any party who fetches the emailed URL (forwarded or leaked link) receives a valid authenticated session, since a state-changing login happens on a GET.
findings.recommendation: Make GET /verify render a confirmation page that performs no state change, and verify+sign-in only on an explicit POST from that page (protected by the same Origin check as /auth/*). At minimum, do not auto-issue a session on GET.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced in the harness against the real gateway: GET /verify?token=... (even with a cross-site Referer and sec-fetch-site:cross-site) returns 303 to / WITH a Set-Cookie session, and a second GET shows the token is burned ('already used' page). So a GET both mints a session and consumes the single-use token, with no Origin/CSRF check (the /verify branch is outside /auth/). Refinements: HEAD /verify falls through to 401 (only GET burns it); and /reset is POST-consumed (POST /auth/reset), so reset links are NOT burned by GET-prefetch — only verification links are. The prefetch-burn half is the operative risk and becomes active once email delivery is turned on (it is currently unconfigured — see missed findings).

findings.title: Account enumeration on signup (email-taken) and login (unverified vs bad-credentials)
findings.location: deploy/railway/auth-routes.mjs:219 (signup -> /signup?error=email-taken) and :229 (login -> /login?error=${attempt.reason}); deploy/railway/auth.mjs:166-181 (reason 'unverified' vs 'bad-credentials')
findings.evidence: Signup returns a distinct error=email-taken when an address already exists, and login returns error=unverified (account exists, not yet verified) vs error=bad-credentials, letting an attacker distinguish registered from unregistered emails and identify unverified accounts. By contrast request-reset (:246) and resend (:264) are deliberately non-enumerating (always ?sent=1 / ?resent=1), so the treatment is inconsistent.
findings.impact: An attacker can confirm which email addresses have iTrack accounts and which are unverified, useful for targeted phishing/credential-stuffing against a public sign-up surface.
findings.recommendation: Decide an enumeration policy for the public product; if minimizing it, collapse the login 'unverified' branch into a neutral 'check your email or your credentials' state (still offering resend from that neutral flow) and consider a generic signup response. This is a known UX/security tradeoff; low severity.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced, with one correction to the mechanism. signup -> /signup?error=email-taken IS a reliable enumeration oracle (works with any password). But login's 'unverified' branch fires ONLY when the supplied password is correct: harness shows login(unverified account, WRONG password) -> bad-credentials, identical to login(unknown email) -> bad-credentials. So login does NOT let an attacker enumerate emails without already knowing the password; the finder overstated the login vector. Net severity P3 is right. The stronger companion enumeration channel is a timing oracle on request-reset (see security-M-... missed), which undercuts the finder's claim that request-reset/resend are 'deliberately non-enumerating'.

findings.title: 5-minute Basic-auth success cache keeps old credentials valid after a password reset
findings.location: deploy/railway/gateway.mjs:14 (BASIC_CACHE_TTL_MS=5m) and :56-93 (basicCache keyed by sha256(username:password)); deploy/railway/auth.mjs:228-237 (resetPassword deletes sessions but cannot reach the in-memory Basic cache)
findings.evidence: On a successful DB Basic auth the identity is cached for 5 minutes keyed by a hash of username:password. resetPassword rehashes the password and deletes all DB sessions, but the gateway's in-process basicCache is not purged, so the previous password's cache entry remains valid until its TTL expires.
findings.impact: After a password reset (often triggered precisely because the old password is compromised), the old credentials continue to grant access via Basic for up to 5 minutes. Scope is limited to Basic clients (the iOS shell).
findings.recommendation: Retire Basic auth together with the iOS shell (removing this cache entirely). Until then, invalidate the user's basicCache entries in resetPassword (e.g. via a shared store/version stamp) or drop the cache TTL substantially.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced precisely: after POST /auth/reset succeeds, store.authenticate(old password) returns bad-credentials, yet a Basic request with the OLD password through the gateway still returns 200 (served from basicCache) for up to the 5-minute TTL. resetPassword deletes DB sessions but cannot reach the in-process basicCache. One correction: this is not strictly iOS-only — ANY Basic client (curl, script, an attacker who knows the old password) benefits, not just the iOS shell. Severity stays P3: 5-minute window, requires knowing the old password.

findings.title: Rate-limiter correctness depends on an unverified assumption about Railway's x-forwarded-for ordering
findings.location: deploy/railway/auth-routes.mjs:70-81 (clientIp uses the LAST XFF entry) feeding signup/login/reset limiters (:141-143) and the gateway basicFailLimiter (gateway.mjs:61,81)
findings.evidence: clientIp trusts the LAST x-forwarded-for entry on the stated assumption that 'Railway's edge APPENDS the real client address as the last entry'. This is validated only by a stubbed unit test; it cannot be confirmed from outside, and XFF ordering is platform-specific. I did not spoof XFF against prod (per the rules).
findings.impact: If Railway instead prepends the client (client-first) and appends internal hops, the last entry is a shared internal IP and all users collapse into one rate-limit bucket (a single abuser throttles everyone / accidental DoS). If the edge does not append at all, the last entry is client-controlled and an attacker mints a fresh budget per request (limiter bypass). The entire limiter's effectiveness rides on this one assumption.
findings.recommendation: Verify empirically with a temporary canary that logs the raw x-forwarded-for from a known client IP, then key on a fixed trusted-proxy hop count rather than a 'last entry' heuristic.
findings.verifier_note: Effectively below a normal P3 (hardening-only) — no vulnerability demonstrated. I could not empirically verify Railway's x-forwarded-for ordering without an XFF-spoof-to-bypass attempt against prod, which the rules preclude. Mitigating facts I DID verify: the service runs a single instance (bound to a /data Railway volume, which forces one replica), so the in-memory limiter state is coherent and there is no cross-replica split; Railway fronts the container with its own edge ('railway-hikari'), which conventionally APPENDS the real peer, matching the code's assumption. The finding is a legitimate 'unverified assumption, verify empirically' hardening note, but it asserts no confirmed bug and the failure modes it hypothesizes are speculative; confidence lowered accordingly.

findings.title: CSRF check on /auth/* permits requests with neither Origin nor Referer (login-CSRF residual)
findings.location: deploy/railway/auth-routes.mjs:171-187 (origin/referer validated only when 'declared' is present; absent => allowed)
findings.evidence: The /auth/* CSRF guard rejects a cross-origin request only when Origin or Referer is present and mismatched; when both are absent the request proceeds. Unlike the app's JSON command endpoint (which also enforces application/json + sec-fetch-site), the form-encoded /auth/login and /auth/signup rely solely on this header check, and SameSite=Lax does not help a login that sets a brand-new cookie.
findings.impact: A client that omits both headers can drive state-changing auth POSTs; the practical residual is login-CSRF (silently logging a victim into an attacker-controlled account). Exploitability is low because modern browsers send Origin on cross-site POSTs.
findings.recommendation: Reject state-changing POSTs to /auth/* when both Origin and Referer are absent, or add a double-submit CSRF token / require a fetch-metadata (sec-fetch-site=same-origin) signal as the JSON endpoint does.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced: POST /auth/login with neither Origin nor Referer returns 303 to / with a Set-Cookie session (state change succeeds). The guard only rejects when a header is present and mismatched — Origin:https://evil -> 403 and Origin:null -> 403 (URL parse throws), but both-absent -> allowed. Residual is login-CSRF. Real-world exploitability is low because modern browsers send Origin on cross-site POSTs; P3 is correct. Fix is one line: reject state-changing /auth/* POSTs when both Origin and Referer are absent.

findings.title: Pre-verification account hijacking / registration squatting, amplified by attacker-controlled lure text in the verification email
findings.location: deploy/railway/auth.mjs:127-143 (createUser, no pre-verification protection) + :217-226 (createResetToken requires verified_at IS NOT NULL) + gateway.mjs:163-173 (GET /verify auto-login) + auth-routes.mjs:212,222 (name accepted 1-80 chars into verificationEmail greeting)
findings.evidence: Reproduced end-to-end in the harness (scenarios.out.txt, section E) against the real modules: (1) Attacker POSTs /auth/signup for victim@ with the attacker's own password and a 'name' of 'URGENT: your RN license lapses Friday - confirm now'; the account is created UNVERIFIED and a verification email is sent to the REAL victim's inbox from the legitimate iTrack sender, with the attacker's string as the greeting ('Hi URGENT: your RN license lapses Friday - confirm now,'). (2) The victim is now locked out: their own signup returns email-taken, request-reset sends nothing (createResetToken requires verified_at NOT NULL), and login with their own password returns bad-credentials. (3) If the victim clicks the link in the email they received, GET /verify auto-logs them in (303 + session) and marks the account verified. (4) The attacker then logs in with the attacker password and the gateway forwards the SAME oai-authenticated-user-email=victim@ to the worker — attacker and victim share one workspace. (5) Attacker can re-lure at will via /auth/resend (fresh 24h link, harness confirmed). Cleanup only removes unverified accounts after 7 days on cron, so squatting is a rolling DoS.
findings.impact: On a public self-serve SaaS, any attacker can (a) permanently block chosen email addresses from ever registering, (b) deliver attacker-authored phishing text to victims inside a genuine iTrack transactional email, and (c) if the victim clicks, share/hijack the victim's professional-license workspace. This is the classic pre-hijack class (CWE-of-account-pre-hijacking).
findings.recommendation: Do not send the verification email with any unverified-user-controlled display name in the body, and treat an unverified email as claimable: on repeat signup for an unverified address, resend to the address instead of returning email-taken, allow password reset to adopt/verify an unverified record, and (critically, ties to security-03) do NOT auto-issue a session on GET /verify — verify then require an explicit login. Cap/scrub the display name used in mail.

findings.title: Transactional email is unconfigured in production: onboarding and password recovery are non-functional and links reach users only via plaintext logs
findings.location: Railway service itrack (prod env) — RESEND_API_KEY and AUTH_EMAIL_FROM are ABSENT from the service variables; deploy/railway/email.mjs:5 (returns email-not-configured when either is unset); deploy/railway/serve.mjs:235-238; auth-routes.mjs:158-166,222-223,245,262
findings.evidence: list_variables on the prod service returns APNS_*, ITRACK_USERS, ITRACK_WIDGET_TOKEN, VAPID_*, RAILWAY_* — but NO RESEND_API_KEY, NO AUTH_EMAIL_FROM, NO PUBLIC_BASE_URL. With both unset, createResendSender returns {ok:false, error:'email-not-configured'} for every message, so every verification and every password-reset email fails to send. Signup then redirects to /signup?sent=1&mail=down whose copy tells the stranger 'the verification email could not be sent. Contact us and we will activate you manually' at support@itrackceu.com — but dig shows itrackceu.com has NO MX record and SMTP ports 25/587 on its A-record IP (69.46.46.121) refuse connections, so that mailbox cannot receive mail. Meanwhile deliver() logs the full single-use link to stdout on failure, so today the ONLY way any account gets verified or reset is by an operator reading Railway logs. This matches the standing open gate in project memory ('GATES: Resend verify itrackceu.com').
findings.impact: A stranger who signs up on the live site cannot verify, cannot reset a password (no account recovery at all), and cannot reach the advertised fallback mailbox — onboarding and recovery are broken for the public product, and every auth secret is currently exposed only through the log stream. This blocks launch of a self-serve SaaS.
findings.recommendation: Provision RESEND_API_KEY + AUTH_EMAIL_FROM (and PUBLIC_BASE_URL) on the prod service with a verified sending domain BEFORE any public launch; stand up a real support@itrackceu.com mailbox (add MX) or change the fallback copy; and stop logging the link (see security-M-03). Note this overlaps the deliverability dimension but the broken-recovery and secrets-only-in-logs facets are security-critical.

findings.title: Single-use verification and password-reset links are written to stdout/Railway logs on any email failure (CWE-532)
findings.location: deploy/railway/auth-routes.mjs:162-164 (deliver(): console.log(`[auth] ${kind} link for ${email}: ${message.link} ...`) on !result.ok), reached from signup:222, request-reset:245, resend:262
findings.evidence: Reproduced in the harness (scenarios.out.txt, section G): with a failing mailer, the process logs `[auth] verification link for g@x.test: https://.../verify?token=<secret> (email send-failed)`. The same path logs reset links. These are the exact single-use secrets that verify an email or set a new password. Anyone with Railway log access, a collaborator, or a configured log drain can read them; a reset link in logs is a full account takeover. Because email is currently unconfigured (security-M-02), this fires on 100% of sends today, not as a rare edge case — and it remains a live risk after email is fixed, since any transient Resend outage re-triggers it.
findings.impact: Exposure of live authentication secrets to the log subsystem; a logged reset link grants password-reset account takeover within its 1-hour TTL (verify links within 24h). Log storage/drains persist them beyond the request.
findings.recommendation: Never log the token or full link. On send failure, log only a non-secret reference (email + kind + token id/hash) and surface a retry/resend path in-product; if a manual-onboarding escape hatch is needed, gate it behind an authenticated admin view rather than stdout.

findings.title: No SPF, DKIM, DMARC (or MX) on itrackceu.com — auth email is spoofable and the domain is phishable
findings.location: DNS for itrackceu.com (authoritative name.com nameservers) — verified via dig @8.8.8.8 and @1.1.1.1
findings.evidence: dig returns empty for TXT itrackceu.com (no SPF), TXT _dmarc.itrackceu.com (no DMARC), TXT resend._domainkey.itrackceu.com and resend._domainkey.send.itrackceu.com (no Resend DKIM), and empty MX. The apex has only an A record to the Railway app IP. So the domain publishes no email-authentication policy at all.
findings.impact: Once transactional mail is enabled, verification/reset emails from an unauthenticated domain are likely to be spam-filtered (hurting the very onboarding the SaaS depends on) and, with no DMARC policy, anyone can spoof mail 'from' itrackceu.com — a strong phishing vector precisely because users are trained to expect iTrack auth emails. For an auth system whose only recovery channel is email, domain authentication is a security control, not just deliverability hygiene.
findings.recommendation: Before enabling email, verify the sending domain in Resend (publish its DKIM CNAME/TXT), add an SPF record authorizing Resend, and publish a DMARC record (start p=none with rua, then tighten to quarantine/reject). Overlaps the deliverability dimension.

findings.title: ITrackApp() is a 4,856-line shell that owns all state, all mutations and nine inline modals
findings.location: app/ITrackApp.tsx:1656-6511 (state 1657-1745; effects 2091-2500; runAction 2598-2671; write handlers 2741-4046; inline modals 4338-6508)
findings.evidence: 43 useState, 10 useRef, 19 useEffect, 10 useMemo, 11 useCallback and 45 inner functions in one component. Nine modals are JSX inside its return, not components: the log sheet (4338-4831) references 38 shell identifiers, credential setup (4875-5376) 29, acceptance 16, allocation 16, submission 15, evidence 14, reminders 12, classification 11, install help 4. The screens are already leaf components (TodayView 6831-7847 with 23 props, CredentialDetailScreen 7938-8365/13, RecordsView 8367-8713/11, AccountView 9143-9600/15) and receive everything by props.
findings.impact: Every screen redesign has to be edited inside the same closure, so screen-by-screen decomposition cannot start until the modals and controller logic are pulled out; none of the business logic (bestNextAction, payload builders, draft lifecycle) is unit-testable in isolation.
findings.recommendation: Follow the 10-step extraction order in ARCHITECTURE-INVENTORY.md section 4.1: pure modules first (types, format, credentialKinds, allocationPayloads, guidedAction), then leaf UI and the three gesture/nav hooks, then screens verbatim, then modals converted to prop-driven components (the ActivityEditorModal pattern: parse FormData synchronously, emit a plain payload), and finally controller hooks (useWorkspace, useMutations, useCatalog, useActivityEntry, usePushDevice, useScreenStack) so ITrackApp.tsx becomes a ~350-line composition root that keeps its filename (the tests locate the built chunk by the `ITrackApp-` prefix).
findings.verifier_note: Re-derived from the file: ITrackApp() spans 1656-6511; occurrence counts are exactly 43 useState / 10 useRef / 19 useEffect / 10 useMemo / 11 useCallback and 45 inner `function` declarations (shell.tsx extract in architecture-verify/). Nine `<Modal` sites live inside the shell's return (4339, 4876, 5379, 5583, 5880, 6027, 6084, 6216, 6382) versus two already-extracted modal components (8774, 9022); the screens are separate functions (TodayView 6831, CredentialDetailScreen 7938, RecordsView 8367, AccountView 9143). I did not re-derive the per-modal identifier counts (38/29/16...). P2 stands.

findings.title: Profile 'Sign out' links to /signout-with-chatgpt, a route that no longer exists (404)
findings.location: app/ITrackApp.tsx:9258-9264; deploy/railway/gateway.mjs:145-220; deploy/railway/auth-routes.mjs:190,234; public/sw.js:22-26
findings.evidence: AccountView renders `Sign out` for every non-demo user. The gateway handles only `/auth/*` (logout is `POST /auth/logout`, auth-routes.mjs:234), `/verify`, and the three page routes; any other path with a valid session is proxied to the worker, which has no such route. GET http://localhost:3000/signout-with-chatgpt on the dev app returns HTTP 404. sw.js still lists `/signin-with-chatgpt` and `/signout-with-chatgpt` as auth paths. Demo users see 'Local preview' instead of the link, which is why it survived; on prod an unauthenticated GET 303s to /login (gateway), so the 404 is only reachable once signed in (not attempted, per rules).
findings.impact: A signed-up user cannot sign out from the app; on a shared or public computer their session (30-day sliding cookie) stays live. For a self-serve public product this is a broken core flow and a trust problem.
findings.recommendation: Replace the anchor with a form that POSTs to `/auth/logout` (or add a GET-safe `/auth/logout` confirmation page in auth-routes.mjs), remove the ChatGPT paths from sw.js AUTH_PATHS, and replace the five 'Sign in with ChatGPT' 401 messages in app/api/**/route.ts and app/api/evidence/_shared.ts:98 with copy that points at /login.
findings.verifier_note: Verified the anchor at ITrackApp.tsx:9260; /auth/* accepts POST only (auth-routes.mjs:190-195 returns 404 for any GET); nothing outside tests references /auth/logout (grep app, deploy, public: 0 hits); GET http://localhost:3000/signout-with-chatgpt returns a plain-text 404 'Not Found' from the worker; on prod with a Safari UA and no cookie the path 303s to /login and GET /auth/logout is 404, so a signed-in user is proxied straight to the worker's 404. Session is a 30-day sliding window (auth.mjs:14, 205-207). Only the demo identity (what the local app shows as 'Local preview') hides the link. No sign-out path exists for a self-serve account, so P1 stands.

findings.title: 165 test assertions are regexes over the source text of ITrackApp.tsx and globals.css, so any file move fails npm test
findings.evidence: AST count over the 2,189 assert calls: 122 mention `clientSource` and 3 `appSource` (both `readFile("../app/ITrackApp.tsx")`) and 40 mention `stylesSource` (`globals.css`), spread over 16 subtests; e.g. `/readNavEntry\(state\)[\s\S]{0,120}?depthRef\.current = entry\?\.depth \?\? 0/` (758), `clientSource.indexOf("function CredentialsView(") < detailStart` ordering (715-726), `/function selectTab\(tab: TabName\) \{\n    hapticTap\(\);/` (981), 38 pins on draft/OCR/push internals (7670-7809), 12 on the catalog chooser (13363-13395), 40 CSS pins such as `/\.screen-pushed \{[^}]*animation: screen-in var\(--screen-push\)/`. `readBuiltClientAppSource()` finds the client chunk by `name.startsWith("ITrackApp-")` and the SSR chunk falls back to the same prefix after trying a stale hardcoded hash `ITrackApp-BvrpzBXC.js`. `npm test` also runs a full `vinext build` first.
findings.impact: Moving any function to a new file breaks a subtest even when behaviour is unchanged; the ordering/adjacency pins cannot be re-pointed at all. Keep the composition root named ITrackApp.tsx so the chunk-prefix lookups keep working.
findings.verifier_note: Reproduced the counts with my own statement parser: 2,189 assert calls, 122 statements reference clientSource, 3 appSource, 40 stylesSource; chunk lookups by the `ITrackApp-` prefix at lines 586 and 1091; the hardcoded `ITrackApp-BvrpzBXC.js` (1082) is stale (dist holds ITrackApp-GObTl6g8.js / ITrackApp-cj8gPdG6.js) so the readdir fallback is what runs today. The cited regexes at 715-726, 758 and 981 exist verbatim. Extra context for the split: the 27,722-line file is a single outer test() with 106 t.test subtests that all import the built worker (dist/server/index.js, line 31), so no subtest can run without the build.

findings.title: One global `error` string and one shared `pending` key serve the page banner and all eleven modal forms
findings.location: app/ITrackApp.tsx:1698-1700 (state), 2598-2671 (runAction sets error for any action key), 4121-4131 (banner), 4793, 5349, 5546, 5844, 5997, 6178, 6344, 6391, 8780, 9028 (per-modal error blocks)
findings.evidence: `setError(` has 54 call sites; every modal renders `{error ? <ModalError title="This activity was not saved" .../>}` from the same variable, and the page banner renders it too when a workspace is loaded. `runAction` writes the error for row-level keys (task, requirement, activity, quest) as well as FORM_ACTION_KEY, so a failed background write that completes after a sheet opens surfaces inside that sheet under the sheet's own title. `pending` is `pendingActionKeys.includes(FORM_ACTION_KEY)` and disables the submit of whichever form is open.
findings.impact: Errors are mis-attributed and every extracted modal will need the shell's error/pending plumbing passed in, which re-creates the coupling the split is meant to remove; also two forms can never be in flight at once by design.
findings.recommendation: Make `runAction` return `{ ok, error, code, id }` instead of writing global state; give each modal its own `useState` for error; have `useMutations` expose `isPending(key)` and let each modal use its own key; reserve the page banner for load failures and row-level errors.
findings.verifier_note: Verified `pending`/`error` state at 1695-1699, runAction writing the single error string for any actionKey (2598-2671), the page banner (4121-4131), seven shell ModalError sites each rendering the same `error` under a different title (4794, 5350, 5547, 5845, 5998, 6179, 6345) and `error={error}` passed into the two extracted modals (4837, 4856). I did not reproduce a user-visible misattribution (it needs a row-level write to fail while a sheet is open); what keeps this at P2 is the verified plumbing every extracted modal will have to inherit.

findings.title: `selectedCredentialId` is a hidden app-wide subject kept in sync by four separate mechanisms, and the Submission/Acceptance modals act on it rather than on the credential the screen shows
findings.location: app/ITrackApp.tsx:1665 (state), 1950-1961 (loadWorkspace fallback), 1807-1893 (sheet capture/restore), 2483-2495 (popstate mirror), 4072-4075 (openCredentialDetail), 3540-3608 (openSubmission/openAcceptance/handleAcceptance use selectedCredential), 4290-4291 and 8303-8342 (detail screen buttons)
findings.evidence: The pushed CredentialDetailScreen is addressed by URL (`stagedDetail`, 2404-2431) but its 'Log submission'/'Record acceptance' buttons call `openSubmission`/`openAcceptance`, which read `selectedCredential` (5378 `submissionOpen && selectedCredential`, 5581). Consistency relies on `openCredentialDetail` setting the selection before `nav.push`, a second popstate listener mirroring the route into the selection, the reminder-launch effect, and `loadWorkspace` re-pointing to the earliest deadline when the id disappears; the log sheet additionally snapshots and restores the selection (selectionBeforeActivityEntry).
findings.impact: Every modal that gets extracted must know which credential it is about; today that knowledge is implicit shell state, so the extracted modal would still reach back into the shell, and the detail screen cannot be made self-contained.
findings.recommendation: Pass the subject explicitly: CredentialDetailScreen calls `onSubmit(credential.id)`, and Submission/Acceptance/Reminders modals take `credential` as a prop; keep `selectedCredentialId` only as Home's 'focused credential' and fold the popstate mirror into useNavigation via an onRouteChange callback.
findings.verifier_note: Verified the state at line 1664 (finder cites 1665, off by one), the loadWorkspace fallback (1951-1960), the popstate mirror (2485-2493), openCredentialDetail (4072-4075), openSubmission/openAcceptance reading selectedCredential (3542-3556), `submissionOpen && selectedCredential` (5378) and the detail screen's onSubmit={openSubmission} (4290). Live: opening 'Log submission' from /credentials/demo-nj-lcsw-2026-... shows the modal for that credential (arch-verify2-report.json) — consistent today only because openCredentialDetail sets the selection before nav.push.

findings.title: event.currentTarget-after-await: zero instances; the guard is by convention in all eight async form handlers
findings.evidence: A brace-balanced scan of every function containing both `await` and `event.currentTarget` finds 0 reads after the first await and 8 synchronous captures: two save `const formElement = event.currentTarget` (3173, 3350) and use it after awaits (3260, 3281, 3360), six build `new FormData(event.currentTarget)` before awaiting. The file-input handlers read `.files` and reset `.value` synchronously before calling the async selection handler. No lint rule enforces this.
findings.impact: Not a bug today; it becomes a regression risk when the nine inline handlers are moved into modal components by hand.
findings.recommendation: When extracting modals, keep form parsing synchronous inside the modal and emit a plain payload through `onSubmit(payload)` (the pattern ActivityEditorModal 8756-8771 and PersonalTaskEditorModal 9012-9019 already use), so no async handler receives the event at all.
findings.verifier_note: The await-based scan is accurate (my brace-balanced scan also finds 8 handlers with await + currentTarget and 0 reads after the first await) but the conclusion 'zero instances, not a bug today' is wrong because the scan only looked at `await`. Five onChange handlers read event.currentTarget.value inside deferred setActivityDraft updaters (ITrackApp.tsx 4521, 4549, 4592, 4630, 4749) and crash the whole app on the second keystroke, reproduced live at 200-300 ms typing speed. Full evidence, mechanism and fix are in architecture-M-01; treat that entry as the replacement for this one rather than counting both.

findings.title: Log activity sheet crashes the entire app on the second keystroke: five onChange handlers read event.currentTarget inside deferred setActivityDraft updaters
findings.location: app/ITrackApp.tsx:4521-4524 (title), 4549-4552 (completionDate), 4592-4603 (totalUnits), 4630-4633 (allocatedUnits), 4749-4752 (provider); pending-lane source app/ITrackApp.tsx:2338-2353 (draft-persist effect: setTimeout 0 ms status update + 250 ms persist); no production boundary: node_modules/vinext/dist/server/app-browser-entry.js:244 (DevRecoveryBoundary only under import.meta.env.DEV)
findings.evidence: Reproduced 8 of 8 multi-keystroke runs on http://localhost:3000/ -> 'Log activity': keyboard.type('12', delay 300 ms) in Credits earned, 'Ethic' at 250 ms in Title, 'NBC' at 200 ms in Provider, and one key in Title then one key in Credits 1.5 s later each throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'value')` at basicStateReducer <- updateReducerImpl <- ITrackApp (dev-transformed ITrackApp.tsx:3066/3149 = source 4523/4593); `.modal-card` goes 1 -> 0 and #main-content is removed (crash-slow-report.json, crash-repro-report.json, crash-units-type.png shows the Vite runtime-error overlay over an empty page). A single keystroke and Playwright fill() (one input event) do not crash because React computes the first update eagerly; after any draft change the persist effect schedules setTimeout state updates, so the next keystroke finds pending lanes, the updater is deferred to render, and React has already nulled event.currentTarget. Not a dev artefact: vinext's dev entry mounts no StrictMode (0 matches) and React's DEV double-invoke (shouldDoubleInvokeUserFnsInHooksDEV, react-dom-client.development.js:8044) is therefore off, which is why the first keystroke survives. The scratchpad dev.log shows the identical TypeError six times from other auditors' sessions (09:06:38-43, 09:31-09:33). The pattern has been in the file since commit f012abb (2026-07-27) and HEAD 3f477e6 is what prod serves (prod landing.html is byte-identical to the repo).
findings.impact: Typing a course title, date, credits, allocated credits or provider — the product's primary flow — unmounts the whole client (dev shows the overlay over an empty page; production has no error boundary of any kind, so the same exception reaches React's root) and the half-typed activity is lost.
findings.recommendation: Read the value synchronously in the handler and pass a plain value into the updater for all five fields, e.g. `const value = event.currentTarget.value; setActivityDraft((current) => ({ ...current, title: value }))` (ActivityEditorModal already does this correctly); add an eslint no-restricted-syntax rule or a rendered-html pin that rejects `event.(currentTarget|target)` inside `set*((x) =>` updaters; and give each extracted sheet its own error boundary so a field bug cannot take the shell down.

findings.title: No error boundary, error.tsx or not-found.tsx anywhere: one render exception blanks the whole app and unknown URLs get a bare 'Not Found'

findings.title: User identity is split across two SQLite stores joined only by an email hash, and there is no account deletion, email change or data export for self-serve users
findings.location: deploy/railway/auth.mjs:59-80 (users/tokens/sessions in /data/auth.db via node:sqlite) and :242 (only deletion is the unverified-account purge); db/identity.ts:8-10, 49-53, 60-75 (worker derives userId = sha256('license-lantern:' + email) from the oai-authenticated-user-* headers); deploy/railway/gateway.mjs:100-107 (headers set on proxy); deploy/railway/auth-routes.mjs:190 (known routes: signup, login, logout, request-reset, reset, resend); db/runtime.ts:6039-6070 (ensureUser upsert)
findings.evidence: grep for delete-account / deleteAccount / change-email / update-email / export-my-data / gdpr across app, deploy, db and worker -> 0 matches; AuthStore has no user delete except `DELETE FROM users WHERE verified_at IS NULL AND created_at < ?`; the worker never receives the auth store's user id, only the email, and upserts its own users row keyed by the email hash on every request, so an email change in auth.db would produce a new empty workspace and an account deletion has to be performed by hand in two databases plus R2. The inter-process header contract still uses the ChatGPT-platform `oai-` names (serve.mjs:7, identity.ts:8-10).
findings.impact: A public self-serve product (decision 2) must be able to delete an account or change an email on request; today no code path exists and the identity join between the gateway and the worker is an undocumented email-hash convention that any future email-edit feature would silently break.
findings.recommendation: Forward the auth store's user id to the worker (e.g. x-itrack-user-id alongside email, keeping the sha256 id as a migration alias), add POST /auth/delete that removes the auth rows and triggers a worker-side purge of users, activities and R2 evidence in one flow, add an email-change route, and rename the oai-* headers in the same change.

findings.title: The gateway answers the app's own JSON fetches with an HTTP Basic challenge once the session lapses, and the client parses that text body as JSON
findings.location: deploy/railway/gateway.mjs:199-216 (fallthrough for any request that is not a Safari/Firefox HTML GET: 401 + WWW-Authenticate: Basic); app/ITrackApp.tsx:1935-1940 (loadWorkspace fetch with accept: application/json), 2614-2620 and 2662-2668 (runAction response.json() and catch); 10897-10915 (WorkspaceLoadFailure handles 401 only for the initial load)
findings.evidence: On prod, `curl -A <Chrome UA> -H 'Accept: application/json' https://itrackceu.com/api/workspace` with no cookie returns `HTTP/2 401`, `content-type: text/plain`, `www-authenticate: Basic realm="iTrack", charset="UTF-8"` (body 'Authentication required'). Every /api/workspace reply is parsed with response.json(), so once a workspace is loaded a lapsed session turns the next save into a SyntaxError surfaced in the banner or the open sheet's ModalError; only the cold-load path has a 401 branch. Browsers raise their native HTTP-auth dialog for same-origin fetch() 401 Basic challenges — I could not observe that live because holding a prod session is out of bounds; the header shape is what I verified.
findings.impact: After the 30-day session expiry, a cleared cookie, or a logout from another tab, a self-serve user mid-task gets a browser credentials popup and a JSON parse error instead of 'sign in again'; the Basic challenge only exists for the retired iOS shell (comment at gateway.mjs:190-198).
findings.recommendation: For /api/* (or any request whose Accept is not text/html) with no session and no Authorization header, return `401 application/json {"error":"authentication_required"}` without WWW-Authenticate, and have runAction/loadWorkspace route a 401 to the sign-in screen; keep Basic only for the ITRACK_USERS bootstrap if still needed. Pairs naturally with the UA-gate removal in architecture-08.

findings.title: app/api/workspace/route.ts is the server-side monolith: 12,504 lines, 138 functions, a 23-case action switch and a 1,115-line getWorkspace, with every mutation followed by a full workspace refetch
findings.location: app/api/workspace/route.ts:4145-5260 (getWorkspace), 12333+ (POST dispatch with 23 `case "<action>":` labels); app/ITrackApp.tsx:2652 (runAction -> loadWorkspace after every success); db/runtime.ts:5998-6037 (initializeDatabase memoised per isolate, so per-request cost is fine)
findings.evidence: `grep -cE '^(export )?(async )?function '` -> 138; 23 distinct case labels; getWorkspace spans 4145-5260; the client performs POST then a full GET after each write, and the GET recomputes the whole workspace server-side (14,053-byte payload for the seeded demo user, arch-verify-report.json). The finder's summary names this module but filed no finding for it.
